title: A training log you can audit
objectives: Build a training log that records everything a rerun needs, and audit one.

screens.title: Two logs, two answers
screens.prose: Two colleagues ran "the same experiment" on our spiral net and got different validation losses. Here are their two training logs, field by field.
screens.question: Tap the row that explains why the two results differ.

hints.text: Look for the one setting that is not the same in both columns.
Every row but two matches; one of those is the result.
The split seed decides which rows train and which validate.

feedback.correct: The split seed: 0 against 1, so the two runs trained and validated on different rows.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Find the setting that differs.

byKey.r7: That row is the result that differs; tap the setting behind it.

explain.text: Everything matches but the split seed. Split 1 gives 0.041 and split 0 gives 0.093: a different 100 validation rows, and a different 400 training rows. Only a log that records the split lets anyone see that.

screens.title: Everything a rerun needs
screens.prose: Name it: a **training log** records everything a rerun needs. That is the configuration and every hyperparameter, all seeds, the data version and split, the code version, losses at fixed intervals, wall time, and every time a test set was scored.
screens.question: Select all that apply: which of these must the log hold so that someone else can rerun the experiment and get the same numbers?

options.text: The code version
Every seed: training and split
The data version
Losses at fixed intervals
Only the final validation loss, to keep the log short
options.why: A final number cannot show a run that blew up and recovered, or where a resume went wrong.

options.text: The best seed's result, with the other seeds dropped
options.why: Dropped seeds hide the spread that l13 asked for.

hints.text: A rerun needs every input that could change a number.
The code, the data and every seed are inputs.
Curves are what you compare against when the rerun disagrees.

feedback.correct: Code, data, every seed and the curve: what the rerun needs and what it is checked against.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask what a stranger would need to reproduce each number.

byKey.final: A final loss alone cannot show where two runs parted.

explain.text: Inputs (code, data, split, seeds, settings) let a rerun start the same way. The curve at fixed steps shows where two runs part, if they do. The test entries show how often the test set was looked at.

screens.title: Write a log entry
screens.prose: Set-up B, run with training seed 4: Adam at 0.015, 300 steps of batch 32, on split seed 0. Its final validation loss was 0.099.
screens.question: Fill in the four missing fields.

hints.text: Read each value from the description above.
Two seeds: one for training, one for the split.
Set-up B runs Adam at 0.015.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Each field is in the description.

byKey.alr: That is set-up A's rate; B runs at 0.015.

explain.text: Both seeds go in, as numbers, not "default". The rate is the setting that makes this B and not A. The final loss sits at the end of the curve, one event among many.

screens.title: Audit a log
screens.prose: A colleague hands you this log for a run they want you to reproduce.
screens.question: Which field is missing?

options.text: The split seed
The code version
The training seed
The loss curve
options.why: The events hold losses at fixed steps.

hints.text: Check the inputs one by one.
Two seeds are needed.
Only one seed is in this log.

feedback.correct: No split seed: the rerun cannot know which rows were validation.

byKey.code: The code version is on line 1.
byKey.seed: The training seed is on line 2.
byKey.curve: The curve is in the events.

explain.text: The log has the training seed but not the split seed. As the two logs above showed, a different split moves the loss nearly as much as a different seed (sd 0.029 against 0.046).

screens.title: Karpathy's recipe
screens.prose: Karpathy's *A Recipe for Training Neural Networks*, in four of its steps. First get the data pipeline right: look at real batches and labels, which catches bad loaders and wrong labels. Then overfit one small batch, which catches a broken model or loss. Then regularise, to close the gap to validation. Then tune.
screens.question: Put the four steps in order. Leave out the one that does not belong.

lines.text: Look at the data and the batches the loader produces
Overfit one small batch to near-zero loss
Add regularisation until validation stops improving
Tune the learning rate and other settings on validation
Score the test set to choose the learning rate
lines.why: The test set is scored once, at the end; choosing anything on it turns it into a validation set.

hints.text: What must work before any loss means anything?
A model that cannot fit 8 points will not fit 400.
Regularise once you can overfit; tune last, on validation.

feedback.correct: Data, overfit, regularise, tune; the test set stays shut.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Each step assumes the one before works.

byKey.o: Check the data before trusting any fit.
byKey.r: Regularise only once the net can overfit.

explain.text: Each step checks what the next relies on: real data, then a model that can learn, then generalisation, then fine settings. The test set is not a step; it is scored once at the end.

screens.title: Overfit one batch
screens.prose: Eight training points, our net, 200 Adam steps at 0.01 on that batch alone. One curve starts from our usual random weights; the other from all weights set to zero, a bug. Slide to reveal the steps.
screens.question: Where does the all-zeros curve sit for all 200 steps? Give 3 decimal places.

hints.text: Read the flat dashed line.
With zero weights every hidden unit is the same and outputs 0.
Four points of each class and no signal give the loss of a coin flip, $\ln 2$.

feedback.correct: 0.693, which is $\ln 2$: the net says 50-50 for every point and never moves.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Read the dashed curve.

byKey.good: That is the random start, which reaches near zero.

explain.text: From a random start the loss on 8 points falls to 0.0004. From zeros every gradient but the last bias is 0, and with four points of each class even that is 0, so the loss stays at $\ln 2 = 0.693$. A net that cannot overfit one batch has a bug.

screens.title: The test set, twice
screens.prose: A log shows the test set scored at step 150. After reading the step-150 test loss, the team lowered the rate from 0.01 to 0.005, the run went on, and the test set was scored again at step 300. The report quotes the second test loss.
screens.question: What is wrong with the reported test loss?

options.text: The first test score chose a change, so the second is no longer a fair test
Nothing: scoring the test set at fixed steps is a curve like any other
options.why: A validation curve is fine; a test curve that steers the run makes the test set a validation set.

options.text: Only that the rate change should be in the config
options.why: Logging the change is right, but the change was chosen by looking at the test set.

hints.text: Why is a test set kept apart?
What did the step-150 score lead to?
`validation` l1 checked that the test rows were touched once.

feedback.correct: The test set steered the run, so its last score is biased downwards.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask what the first test score was used for.

byKey.fine: A test score that steers the run is not a test.
byKey.rate: The change was logged; the problem is what chose it.

explain.text: The test set was looked at, a setting changed, and the same test set judged the result. That is `validation` l1's touched test set. The log is what lets an auditor see it: count the test entries.

screens.title: Edge case: stopped and resumed
screens.prose: Set-up A, seed 0, stopped at step 150 and resumed from a checkpoint. Restoring the weights, Adam's moments and step count, and the batch generator's state gives 0.0927, as the run that never stopped. Restarting the batch stream from the seed gives 0.1279; also resetting Adam gives 0.1101.
screens.question: What must the log show for the resumed run?

options.text: Both segments, the checkpoint step, and that the optimiser and generator states were restored
Only the final validation loss, since the second segment is where the run ends
options.why: The final loss cannot show whether the resume repeated batches or reset Adam.

options.text: Only the second segment and its curve, since it produced the final weights
options.why: The first segment made the checkpoint the second starts from.

hints.text: Which resumes changed the result?
A restarted stream repeats the first 150 batches.
The log must show what was restored, and both halves of the curve.

feedback.correct: Both segments, where it stopped, and what state came back: then a rerun can follow it.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask what a rerun would need to land on the same number.

byKey.final: Three resumes, three final losses: the final number alone cannot tell them apart.

explain.text: Only a full restore reproduces 0.0927; the other resumes moved the result by up to 0.035, as much as a new seed. So the log records the stop, the checkpoint, the restored states and both segments of the curve.

screens.title: An audit in code
screens.prose: Write `audit_log(log)` for logs shaped like ours: top-level fields, and `events`, each with a `step` and a `kind` of `"loss"`, `"test"`, `"set"` or `"resume"`. The comments in the starter give the exact problems and their order.
screens.question: Write `audit_log`.

widget.starter:
REQUIRED = ["code", "data", "split_seed", "seed", "config"]


def audit_log(log):
    # return the list of problems, in this order:
    #   "missing <field>" for each REQUIRED field absent or None, in REQUIRED order
    #   "no loss curve" when fewer than 2 loss events
    #   "test scored <k> times" when k > 1 test events
    #   then, event by event: "changed <key> at step <step>" for a set event,
    #   "resume at step <step> without a checkpoint" for a resume event with no "from"
    ...

tests.expect: ['missing seed', 'test scored 3 times', 'changed p at step 100']

widget.how: `BASE` is a clean log of set-up A, seed 0, and `variant(...)` plants faults in a copy. Submit runs 8 hidden tests on planted logs: clean, missing fields, a second test score, a setting changed, the final loss only, a resume with and without a checkpoint, and two mixes. Each list must match exactly, in order.

mutants.symptom: Counts the one allowed test score as a problem.
Misses a field that is present but None.
Sorts the problems instead of keeping the stated order.

hints.text: Fields first, then the events.
A field set to `None` is as missing as an absent one.
Count test events once; walk the events in order for set and resume.

feedback.correct: All pass: your audit finds every planted fault, in order.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Read the first failing test in the results.

screens.title: Overfit one batch, in code
screens.prose: Write `overfit_one_batch(make_net, batch, steps, lr)`: build `params = make_net()`, train them on the one batch with `loss_and_grads` and `adam_step` (step numbers from 1), and return `full_loss` on the batch after the last step. Our net should end near zero; the zero net cannot.
screens.question: Write `overfit_one_batch`.

widget.starter:
import numpy as np
from nt_ops_l1 import loss_and_grads, full_loss, adam_step


def overfit_one_batch(make_net, batch, steps, lr):
    # train make_net() on the one batch (Xb, yb) with Adam for `steps` steps; return the final loss on that batch
    ...
widget.solution:
import numpy as np
from nt_ops_l1 import loss_and_grads, full_loss, adam_step


def overfit_one_batch(make_net, batch, steps, lr):
    Xb, yb = batch
    params = make_net()
    m = [np.zeros_like(p) for p in params]
    v = [np.zeros_like(p) for p in params]
    for t in range(1, steps + 1):
        _, grads = loss_and_grads(params, Xb, yb)
        params, m, v = adam_step(params, grads, m, v, t, lr)
    return full_loss(params, Xb, yb)
widget.how: The data files and `autograd.py`, `nt_ops_l1.py` to `nt_ops_l4.py` are in the working directory. `BATCH` holds 8 training points, `make_net()` our usual start and `zero_net()` all zeros. Submit runs 5 hidden tests: a 5-step run exactly (relative $10^{-7}$), below 0.01 after 200 steps, the zero net stuck above 0.6, no steps at all, and a second batch.

import numpy as np
from nt_ops_l1 import loss_and_grads, full_loss, adam_step


def overfit_one_batch(make_net, batch, steps, lr):
    Xb, yb = batch
    params = make_net()
    m = [np.zeros_like(p) for p in params]
    v = [np.zeros_like(p) for p in params]
    for t in range(1, steps + 1):
        last, grads = loss_and_grads(params, Xb, yb)
        params, m, v = adam_step(params, grads, m, v, t, lr)
    return loss_and_grads(params, Xb, yb)[0] if steps == 0 else last
mutants.symptom: Returns the loss measured before the last step.

`adam_step` returns new parameters; keep them.
Step numbers run 1 to `steps`, and the loss is measured after the last step.

feedback.correct: All pass. After 200 steps our net is at 0.0004 on its 8 points; the zero net never leaves $\ln 2$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Read the first failing test in the results.

screens.title: After a bad month
screens.prose: A model behind a live strategy had a bad month, and the risk committee asks whether last year's training did what the research note said. The team kept one of two records.
screens.question: Which record lets the team rerun last year's training and show it?

options.text: A log of the code version, data and split, seeds, settings, curves and one test score
The research note's slide with the final validation and test losses of the model
options.why: Two final numbers cannot be rerun: the inputs that made them are missing.

options.text: The final trained weights of the live model, saved to disk with a date
options.why: Weights show what was shipped, not how it was trained, so the training cannot be rerun or checked.

hints.text: Rerunning needs the inputs, not the outputs.
Which record names the code, data and seeds?
The curves let the rerun be checked step by step.

feedback.correct: Only the full log lets the team rerun the training and compare it, curve for curve.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask what a rerun needs.

byKey.weights: Weights are an output, not a recipe.

explain.text: With the code, data, split, seeds and settings the team retrains last year's model and checks the curve matches the logged one. Then the bad month is a question about the market, not about whether the model was what it claimed.

ideas: A training log records everything a rerun needs: configuration, every seed, data version and split, code version, losses at fixed steps, wall time and every test score.
Karpathy's recipe: get the data right, overfit one small batch, then regularise, then tune; a net that cannot overfit 8 points has a bug.
A resume must restore the optimiser and generator states and log both segments: restarting the batch stream moved our loss from 0.093 to 0.128.

formula.name: Audit rules
formula.note: And no input missing: code, data, split seed, seed, configuration.

summary.trap: A log with the final loss only, or a test set scored more than once.

quiz.prose: A log holds the code version, the data version, the training seed, the configuration and a loss curve.
quiz.question: What is still missing for an exact rerun on our set-up?

options.text: The split seed
The wall time of the run
options.why: Wall time is worth logging, but a rerun does not need it to get the same numbers.

options.text: A picture of the loss curve
options.why: The curve is already there as numbers.

feedback.correct: Without the split seed the rerun cannot rebuild the validation rows.

byKey.wall: Wall time does not change any number.

explain.text: Our runs use two seeds: one for training and one for the split. The log has only the first.

quiz.prose: A new net is trained on one batch of 8 points for 500 steps. Its loss on that batch stays at 0.69.
quiz.question: What does that tell you?

options.text: Something is broken: a working net memorises 8 points
It needs more regularisation before it can fit
options.why: Regularisation makes fitting harder, not easier; it comes after overfitting works.

options.text: It needs more data to learn the pattern
options.why: More data makes memorising harder; 8 points should be easy.

feedback.correct: A net that cannot overfit 8 points has a bug in the model, loss or optimiser.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask what a working net does to 8 points.

byKey.reg: Regularise only after the net can overfit.
byKey.data: More data is the opposite of the test.

explain.text: A loss of 0.69, about $\ln 2$, means it still says 50-50. Karpathy's second step catches exactly this before any long run.

quiz.prose: A training log lists test-set scores at steps 100, 200 and 300.
quiz.question: How many times should a test set be scored in a run whose test loss is reported?

feedback.generic: Not quite. The test set reports once.

byKey.three: Three looks let the test set steer the run.
byKey.zero: It is scored once, or there is nothing to report.

explain.text: The test set is scored 1 time, after every choice is made. Curves during training use the validation set.
